The first, which is the school of Sībawayh: «لا» is negative in the sense of laysa, and the tāʾ is added to it, as it is added in rubba and thamma; it operates only on times in particular, such as lāta ḥīna and lāta awāna, as in the saying:
3830 - They sought our peace, and it was no time (lāta awānin), so we answered that it is not a time for survival
and the saying of another:
3831 - The aggressors regretted, and it was no hour of regret (lāta sāʿata mandami); and aggression is a pasture whose seeker is unwholesome
Most often its nominative is omitted, its estimation being: "wa-lāta l-ḥīnu ḥīna manāṣin." Sometimes the accusative is omitted and the nominative retained; some read here so, as in the saying: 3832 - Whoever turned away from their fires, I am the son of Qays, there is no leaving (lā barāḥ), that is: "there is no leaving for me." It does not operate on other than times, according to the well-known view, but some have clung to its operating on other than times by the saying:
3833 - Nawār yearned, and it was not the place (lāta hannā) to yearn; and what Nawār had hidden appeared
For «hannā» is among the adverbs of place. There is irregularity in it in three respects: one, its operating on a demonstrative, which is definite, while it operates only on indefinites; the second, its being non-declinable; the third, its not being a time. Some have rejected this: «hannā» has departed from place and been used for time, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: {هُنَالِكَ ابتلي المؤمنون} [al-Aḥzāb: 11] and the saying of the poet:
3834 - ... for there they confess: where is the refuge?
as preceded in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb; but the other two irregularities remain. Some interpreted the line in another way: that «lāta» here is disregarded and does not operate, and «hannā» is an adverbial, a fronted khabar, / and «ḥannat» is a mubtadaʾ by interpretation with the maṣdarī «an» omitted, its estimation: "an ḥannat," like «تَسْمَعُ بالمُعَيْدِيِّ خيرٌ مِنْ أَنْ تَراه». In this there is strain and remoteness, except that it has relief from the mentioned irregularities, or two irregularities.
In stopping on it there are two schools. The well-known one among the Arabs and the majority of the Seven Readers is with the extended tāʾ, following the written form of the noble copy. Al-Kisāʾī alone of the Seven stops with hāʾ. The first is the school of al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Zajjāj, al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Kaysān; the second is the school of al-Mubarrad. Abū ʿUbayd was strange, saying: one stops at «لا» and the tāʾ is attached to «حين», so they say: qumtu taḥīna qumta, and taḥīna kāna kadhā faʿaltu kadhā. He said: "I saw it in the imām [the Uthmānic codex] so: «ولا تحين» connected." He also recited as evidence the saying of the poet:
3835 - Those who show kindness at the time (taḥīna) when there is no one showing kindness, and the feeders in the time when there is no feeder
But the codices are only «ولاتَ حين». The majority took what he saw as one of the irregularities of the orthographic norm, like its parallels that have passed.
As for the line, it was said: it is irregular and no attention is paid to it. It was also said: when the ḥīn annexed to the sentence containing «lāt» is omitted, it is permissible that «lā» alone be omitted and be dispensed with by the tāʾ. The original: "al-ʿāṭifūna ḥīna lāta ḥīna lā min ʿāṭifin," so the first «ḥīn» and «lā» alone were omitted, just as the annexation of «ḥīn» to it is explicit in the saying of another: 3836 - And that was when it was no time (ḥīna lāta awāna) for forbearance ... [incomplete in the source]
Ibn Mālik mentioned this view, and it is very forced. The annexation of «ḥīn» to it may also be estimated without omission of it, as in the saying:
3837 - He remembered the love of Laylā, it being no time (lāta ḥīnā) ... [incomplete in the source]
that is: "ḥīna lāta ḥīn." Also, what would Abū ʿUbayd do with his saying:
3838 - ... [incomplete in the source] and it was no hour of regret (wa-lāta sāʿata mandami)
[and his saying]:
3839 - ... lāta awāna ... [incomplete in the source]
for the tāʾ has been found with «lā» without «ḥīn»?
The second of the preceding views: that it operates as «inna» operates, meaning that it is a negator of the genus, so «ḥīna manāṣin» is its ism and its khabar is implied, its estimation: "wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣin lahum," as you say lā ghulāma safarin laka; and its ism is declined because it is an annexed noun.
The third: that after it there is an implied verb putting «ḥīna manāṣ» in the accusative, that is: "lāta araā ḥīna manāṣin lahum," meaning "I do not see that," and like it: {لاَ مَرْحَباً بِهِمْ} and "lā ahlan wa-lā sahlan," that is: they did not come to a welcome, nor meet a family, nor tread an easy ground. Al-Akhfash held these two views and they are weak. The implying of the verb here is not like its implying in the saying:
3840 - Would that there were a man, may Allah reward him well ... [incomplete in the source]
of necessity, because its ism, a single indefinite, is indeclinable on fatḥa; so when we saw this declined, we estimated a verb for it. This is contrary to al-Zajjāj, who permits its tanwīn in poetic necessity, and claims that its fatḥa is for declension, and that the tanwīn was omitted only for lightness, and argues by the line mentioned; its verification has preceded.
The fourth: that this «lāt» is not «lā» to which the tāʾ of feminine is added, but is rather «laysa», with the sīn replaced by tāʾ; they replaced it in places: they said al-nāt, meaning al-nās. From it also sitt, the original being sids. He said:
3841 - May Allah fight the sons of al-Saʿlāt, ʿAmr ibn Yarbūʿ, the worst of the people (al-nāt), they are neither good nor shrewd (akyāt)
It was also read irregularly «قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ النات» to the end. He meant: shirār al-nās, and lā akyās, so he replaced. When he replaced the sīn with tāʾ, he feared its confusion with the particle of wishing, so he turned the yāʾ into alif, leaving «lāt»; this is of the category of sufficing with the letter of weakness, because the weak letter turns into alif only under conditions, among them that it has a vowel and what precedes it has fatḥa. So «ḥīna manāṣ» is its khabar, the ism being omitted as preceded, and the operation here is by right of originality, not derivation.
ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read {وَّلاَتِ حِينِ مَنَاصٍ} with kasra on the tāʾ and genitive «ḥīn», and this reading is / very problematic. Al-Farrāʾ claimed that «lāt» governs the genitive, and recited:
3842 - ... and you will surely regret, and it will be no hour of regret (wa-lāta sāʿati mandami)
and another recited:
3843 - They sought our peace, and it was no time (wa-lāta awānin) ... [incomplete in the source]
the line. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Like it is the saying of Abū Zubayd al-Ṭāʾī: 'They sought our peace', the line. He said: If you say, what is the reason for the genitive in «awān»? I say: it is likened to «idh» in the saying:
3844 - ... and you, at that time (idhin), are healthy
in that it is a time from which the annexed noun was cut off and tanwīn was given in exchange for it, for the original is 'wa-lāta awāna ṣulḥin.' If you say: what do you say about «ḥīna manāṣin», while the annexed noun is present? I say: he treated the cutting of the annexed noun from «manāṣ» (because its origin is ḥīna manāṣihim) as the cutting of it from «ḥīn», because of the unity of the muḍāf and muḍāf ilayhi, and made its tanwīn a compensation for the omitted muḍāf; then he made the ḥīn indeclinable for being annexed to a non-declinable." End.
The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] derived it from the implying of «min», the original being: "wa-lāta min ḥīni manāṣ," so «min» was omitted and its operation remained, like their saying: ʿalā kam jidhʿin banayta baytaka? that is: min jidhʿ, in the sounder of the two views. There is another view in it: that the genitive is by annexation, and like it is the saying:
3845 - Would that there were a man (alā rajulin), may Allah reward him well ... [incomplete in the source]
they recited it with the genitive of «rajul», that is: "alā min rajulin."
I say: it may be supported by its appearance in the saying:
3846 - ... and he said: Indeed, there is no way (lā min sabīl) to Hind
He said: "And the position of «min ḥīni manāṣ» is nominative as the ism of «lāt» in the sense of laysa, as you say laysa min rajulin qāʾiman, and the khabar is omitted; on this is the saying of Sībawayh. And on the basis that it is a mubtadaʾ and the khabar omitted, on the saying of al-Akhfash. Al-Akhfash derived «ولاتَ أَوانٍ» on an omitted muḍāf, meaning: the muḍāf was omitted and the muḍāf ilayhi remained genitive as it was. The original is: wa-lāta ḥīnu awānin."
Makkī rejected this view: the muḍāf ilayhi should have stood in its place in i'rab and been put in the nominative. I say: the remaining of the muḍāf ilayhi in the genitive has occurred. It is of two kinds: little and much. The much is that there be in the wording one like the muḍāf, such as:
3847 - Do you reckon every man a man, and many a fire kindled by night a fire?
that is: "and every fire." The little is that there be not, like the reading of those who read {والله يُرِيدُ الآخرة} with genitive on «al-ākhira»; let this be of it. Though al-Mubarrad reported it in the nominative, by putting it in place of the muḍāf.
Al-Zajjāj said: "The original: wa-lāta awānanā, so the muḍāf ilayhi was omitted, so it must not be declined, and its kasra is for the meeting of two sukūns." The Shaykh said: "This is the view that al-Zamakhsharī established, taking it from Abū Isḥāq." I say: he means the first view, namely his saying: wa-lāta awāna ṣulḥin.
This is what concerns the genitive of «ḥīn».
As for the kasra of the tāʾ of «lāt», it is on the basis of the meeting of two sukūns, like jayri, except that a feminine tāʾ is known only with fatḥa.
ʿĪsā also read with kasra on the tāʾ only, and the accusative «ḥīn» like the majority. He also read «ولات حينُ» in the nominative, «مناصَ» with fatḥa. This is a very problematic reading, not far from error on the part of its transmitter from ʿĪsā, for he is of a standing in knowledge that would prevent him from such a reading. Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī derived it in his «Lawāmiḥ» on fronting and delaying, and that «ḥīn» was treated like qabl and baʿd in being indeclinable on ḍamma when cut off from annexation, by the common ground between it and them in temporal adverbiality. And «manāṣa» is its ism, indeclinable on fatḥa, separated from it by «ḥīn» cut off from annexation. / The original: wa-lāta manāṣa ḥīni kadhā, then the muḍāf ilayhi «ḥīn» was omitted and made indeclinable on ḍamma, and fronted as a separator between «lāt» and its ism. He said: "It may be that there is a meaning in that which I do not know." It has been reported of the tāʾ of «lāt»: fatḥa, kasra and ḍamma.
And His saying: «فنادَوْا» has no object, for the intention is that they performed calling, without intending a particular one called. Al-Kalbī said: "When they fought and were forced, they would call to one another: 'manāṣ,' that is: 'take to flight'; so when the punishment came to them, they said: 'manāṣ.' Then Allah the Exalted said to them: 'wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣin'." Al-Qushayrī said: "On this the estimation is: 'so they called out: manāṣ,' and it was omitted because what follows indicates it." I say: so the called one is omitted, which is some of them, and what they called with, which is "manāṣ," that is: they called one another with this expression. Al-Jurjānī said: "That is: 'so they called out when there was no escape,' that is: at the hour when there is no deliverance and no escape; when he fronted «lā» and delayed «ḥīn», this required the wāw, as the ḥāl requires when it is made a mubtadaʾ and khabar, like when you say 'jāʾa Zaydun rākiban' and then say 'jāʾa wa-huwa rākibun'. So «ḥīn» is an adverbial of His saying «فنادَوْا»." The Shaykh said: "That the origin of this sentence is 'fa-nādaw: ḥīna lā manāṣ', and that «ḥīn» is an adverbial of His saying «فنادَوْا», is a non-Arabic claim on the composition of the Qur'an, and the meaning on its composition is utterly clear." I say: al-Jurjānī does not mean that ḥīn is an adverbial of «نادَوْا» in the construction the Qur'an now has; he means that only in the original meaning and construction, as he likened it to your saying «جاء زيدٌ راكباً» and then «جاء زيدٌ وهو راكب»: «راكباً» in the first construction is a ḥāl, and in the second a khabar of a mubtadaʾ; likewise «ḥīn» was originally an adverbial of the calling, then became the khabar of «lāt» or its ism, according to the disagreement above.
Al-manāṣ: of the pattern mafʿal, from nāṣa yanūṣu, that is: he fled, so it is a maṣdar. One says nāṣahu yanūṣuhu when he escaped him; this is transitive. And nāṣa yanūṣu, that is: he lagged behind; from it nāṣa ʿan qirnihi, that is: he lagged behind from his opponent out of cowardice. Al-Farrāʾ said it, and recited the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
3848 - Is it from remembering Salmā, because she is far from you, that you flee? Then you fall short of her for a while and go forward
Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās said: "nāṣa yanūṣu, that is: he advanced, so it is among the contronyms (aḍdād)." And istanāṣa: he sought the manāṣ. Ḥāritha ibn Zayd said:
3849 - Full of pace when I shorten his rein with my two hands, he sought escape and desired the running of the mishal
One says: nāṣa ilā kadhā yanūṣu nawṣan, that is: he took refuge in it.
